tier_reason: Tier stays C (first-party 2016 tables). Enricher found the 'Dino best' rows for fact and fib use !pure result caching, so those ratios compare a cache lookup against full recursion; the fair comparison is the plain-Dino row.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 2016 README tables (Dino 0.98, Python 3.4, Ruby 2.1), relative times with plain Dino (no hints) as the fair reference: Loop Python 257 vs Dino 19 (13.5x), Fact 90.4 vs 13.2 (6.8x), Fib 492 vs 112 (4.4x), Method 5.8 vs 1.0, Object 4.4 vs 1.0, Sieve 37.9 vs 1.0, Thread 125 vs 1.0, Hash 2.4 vs 1.0; Ruby 157/25.2/142/1.5/1.4/4.5/43.6/2.2. corrections.caveats: First-party 2016 tables from DINO/compare.tst: one run per variant, user CPU time only, base taken as the minimum over the plain, -O and hint variants; the Fact and Fib best rows use !pure, which caches pure-function results (preprint section 3.3.2), so the best run does a cache lookup while Python and Ruby run the full recursion. Default build is -Ofast (implies -ffast-math) plus -flto. Python wins fact and hash on ARM, Ruby wins loop on PPC64. Abandoned since 2019-11-19; GPL-2.0-or-later plus LGPL-2.0-or-later.

corrections.caveats: Indirect evidence: pg_jitter's AsmJit backend against PostgreSQL's llvmjit, not the library itself; the 'up to 32%' figure is against the interpreter. Do not quote the Wide1K rows: pg_jitter 0.3.0 skipped deform JIT for them, so asmjit runs at 0.97-0.98x the interpreter while llvmjit pays 983-2043 ms of compile time. pg_jitter creates a fresh JitRuntime (64 kB block) per expression and counts it as compile time. MIR compiles faster on Wide100 and Wide300 and sljit is about 2x faster on almost every query. Backends: x86, x86-64, AArch64 only (no AArch32).
